summary: Introduces the v6ops project to document all uses of IPv4 addresses in IETF standards-track and experimental RFCs. It explains the method, which RFC types were covered, and summarizes results across seven area documents. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3789 introduces an Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) project that searched protocol specifications for dependencies on IPv4 addresses. It explains which documents were included, how the survey was done, and how results were divided by area.

subtitle: An introduction to the IETF survey of IPv4 dependencies in standards-track and experimental RFCs.

tldr.problem: Protocols written for IPv4 may assume IPv4 addresses in ways that affect later transition work. The IETF survey aimed to identify where those dependencies appeared in standards-track and experimental RFCs.
tldr.mechanism: The project examined RFC text, excluded Informational, BCP and Historic documents, and organized results into seven documents by IETF area.
tldr.outcome: The initial survey identified IPv4 dependencies in 173 of 877 RFCs. RFC 3789 introduces the method and summarizes results; the seven area documents contain the detailed surveys.

today: RFC 3789 is an Informational introduction to the seven-document IPv4 survey. It summarizes the survey method and initial results but does not prescribe changes to the surveyed protocols.

sections.title: Why the IETF Surveyed IPv4 Use
sections.content:
The v6ops project documented uses of IPv4 addresses in IETF standards-track and experimental RFCs. Its purpose was to make dependencies visible while the Internet community considered the transition to IPv6. RFC 3789 is the introduction to a set of seven area-specific survey documents.

The introduction also comments that standards classifications had not been actively maintained for older documents. It notes that a Historic label does not necessarily mean a protocol is unused, using RIP version 1 as an example stated in the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The project looked for places where Internet specifications depended on IPv4 addresses. This RFC introduces the project and explains why the documents were grouped by technical area.

sections.title: How the Survey Was Conducted
sections.content:
The study examined Full, Draft and Proposed Standards, as well as Experimental RFCs. It excluded Informational RFCs, Best Current Practice documents, and Historic RFCs; it also excluded RFCs that had been obsoleted.

The authors describe an exhaustive reading of the applicable specifications, totaling approximately 25,000 pages. They tried to determine whether each RFC depended on IPv4, rather than simply counting every mention of an IPv4 address.
sections.plainLanguage: The survey read the selected documents rather than relying on titles or summaries. It excluded several document categories and tried to identify actual dependencies on IPv4 addresses.

sections.title: Survey Results by IETF Area
sections.content:
The initial survey identified 173 RFCs with an IPv4 dependency among 877 examined. The RFC reports different totals for each area: Application, Internet, Operations and Management, Routing, Security, Sub-IP, and Transport. For example, it reports 23 positives among 46 Routing Area RFCs and 4 among 124 Security Area RFCs.

The authors define a positive as an RFC containing an IPv4 dependency, regardless of context. They note that some identified documents might need no action, while others might be updated by the relevant working groups.
sections.plainLanguage: The survey found IPv4 dependencies in 173 of the 877 documents it examined. The number varied by technical area, and finding a dependency did not automatically mean that a document needed to change.

sections.title: Long-Term Address Stability and Limits
sections.content:
The RFC says a full analysis of how changing addresses affect protocols is beyond its scope. It raises a design question: transport protocols such as TCP and UDP do not provide a mechanism for a connection to continue through an orderly change of endpoint address.

This discussion is exploratory, not a specification or conclusion that a particular protocol must change. The RFC's security considerations state that examining IPv6 readiness does not itself raise security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The survey raises a broader question about how protocols handle changes to endpoint addresses. It does not define a solution or require a particular protocol change.
